title: ADHD floordrobe: why clothes end up on the floor (and the fix)
description: An ADHD floordrobe happens because out of sight is out of mind. Two working-memory studies explain why, plus the See-to-Keep Method that fixes it.
h1: The ADHD floordrobe: why your clothes end up on the floor (and the fix that actually works)
target_query: what is a floordrobe and how do I fix mine if I have ADHD

faq.q: What is a floordrobe, and how do I fix mine if I have ADHD?
faq.a: A floordrobe is when your clothes and belongings live on the floor instead of in a closet or drawers. For ADHD brains it isn't laziness, it's a workaround for weak working memory: if something is out of sight it feels gone, so you leave it in view where you can still find it. The fix is visible storage, clear bins, hooks at eye level, one basket per room, not more discipline.

faq.q: Why do I keep everything on the floor with ADHD?
faq.a: Because out of sight is genuinely out of mind for ADHD brains. Closing a drawer or a wardrobe door can make an item disappear from your working memory, so your brain keeps things visible as insurance against forgetting. The floor is just the biggest, easiest shelf in the room. The fix is visible storage, not more discipline.

faq.q: How do I stop the ADHD floordrobe?
faq.a: Stop hiding things and start storing them in the open. Swap opaque drawers for clear bins, put hooks where your eyes already land, and give each room one visible laundry basket. When away and visible become the same thing, the floor loses its job. Then do a quick five-minute floor reset to catch up.

sources.supports: A meta-analysis of 38 studies found consistent working memory deficits in adults with ADHD, the measured mechanism behind the out-of-sight, out-of-mind experience that turns the floor into a shelf.

A meta-analysis of 83 studies (3,734 people with ADHD vs 2,969 without) found working memory among the most consistent executive-function deficits in ADHD, with effect sizes in the medium range (.46 to .69).

Barkley's model names working memory as one of four executive functions that depend on behavioral inhibition, the theoretical link between an inhibition deficit and losing track of things once they're out of view.
